prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks that brought frequency measurement to the 10^-18 level
for the conception and leadership of the IceCube observatory and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest case on the shortlist. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removed the Doppler and recoil limits, and Ye's strontium systems and clock comparisons took accuracy and stability to 10^-18. Independent clocks at several national laboratories agree, and the redefinition of the second is on a concrete roadmap. Six members rank it, and I agree with the four who rank it first that it is the strongest single achievement. I now put it at the top of my configuration, ahead of my own opening first choice. I keep IceCube as the second part because it is a different kind of discovery. A cubic-kilometre detector in Antarctic ice established a diffuse high-energy astrophysical neutrino flux, and later analyses tied neutrinos to TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane. This is a new observational window, confirmed by several independent analyses and channels over a decade. Pairing a metrology prize with an astroparticle prize keeps the union at three people and spreads the award across two distinct fields rather than adding a third atomic-physics or condensed-matter case.
statement.case_against: The IceCube part rests on one credited name for an enterprise of hundreds of people. Halzen's leadership is real, but the early proposers, the detector builders and the analysts who established the diffuse flux are not in the credited list, so a single-name part is exposed on attribution. The source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) are statistically less secure than the diffuse flux, and the committee could reasonably call neutrino astronomy a few years short of a prize. Opening support is thin, with two members ranking it. Separately, a clocks-only prize is cleaner. Katori and Ye already have broad support on the committee, and attaching a weakly supported second part could dilute it. If colleagues find the IceCube attribution unconvincing, I would drop to B001 alone before I would add a different second part with weaker support.

responses.point: Optical lattice clocks (Katori, Ye) rank first because progress is limited by what can be measured and how accurately, with independent labs confirming 1e-18 and the SI redefinition approaching.
responses.response: I agree and have moved the clocks to the top of my configuration. Your measurement-first criterion also applies to IceCube, since its detector is the discovery tool. I disagree mildly on timing. The redefinition of the second is a metrology decision and does not by itself show new physics, so the prize should be justified on the instrument and on what it already measured. Your point that Hall and Hänsch were recognised in 2005 for the comb is also the main reason I keep the credit to Katori and Ye and not to a larger group.

responses.point: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B017) is ranked first as a concrete prediction followed by a decisive experiment, with timely recognition about eight years after the experiment.
responses.response: The theory-plus-experiment structure is attractive and I rank B017 as my first alternative. I do not put it in my preferred configuration for two reasons. You and Eva Olsson both note that the pairing mechanism is unsettled and that Yuan Cao as first author is outside the credited names, so the attribution is awkward. Your own list also ranks IceCube fourth, and I read that as some sympathy for neutrino astronomy. I would like to hear whether you see B027 as complementary to a clocks prize or only as a lower-ranked option.

responses.point: Circuit QED (B003) is ranked first because it is the architecture on which essentially all superconducting quantum processors and microwave quantum optics now rest.
responses.response: I rank circuit QED third and keep it as an alternative. My reservation is timing. The 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is close in subject matter, and giving cQED so soon afterwards risks reading as a second prize for one platform. Four names are credited and only three can be chosen, so Girvin is left out of any workable configuration. If you can show that the strong-coupling and dispersive-readout results stand apart from the 2025 work, that would shift my view.

responses.point: The Higgs discovery (B002) is central and arguably overdue for experimental recognition, with Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee as the conceivers and builders of the detectors.
responses.response: I accept the scientific importance and the maturity of the case. My difficulty is attribution. Thousands of collaborators made the discovery and the credited trio is only one reading of who conceived and led it; Gianotti, Incandela and Heuer could also be argued for. As an experimentalist I find that choice hard to defend as a decisive-contribution case, so I do not include B002 even as an alternative. I would not oppose it if the committee settles the attribution.

uncertainties: Whether a single-name IceCube credit for Halzen is defensible given the size of the collaboration and the omitted early proposers and builders.
Whether the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 source associations are mature enough, or whether the case should rest on the diffuse flux alone.
Whether the committee prefers a clocks-only prize to a two-part prize, which would drop B027.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001 or B027. I work in astroparticle physics, so I know the neutrino field and its instrumentation, but my documented collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur) do not include IceCube, and I have no recorded tie to Halzen, Katori or Ye. My professional proximity to B027 should be taken into account when weighing my advocacy for it.
